implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent separates the two halves of the decision. The bound is the collection: ArrayBlockingQueue is documented as "a classic bounded buffer" whose put blocks, offer returns false, offer(e, timeout, unit) bounds the wait and add throws IllegalStateException when full. The policy can then be lifted into an object: ThreadPoolExecutor's four predefined RejectedExecutionHandler strategies - AbortPolicy (throw RejectedExecutionException), CallerRunsPolicy (run in the submitting thread, i.e. back-pressure), DiscardPolicy and DiscardOldestPolicy (lose work, deliberately) - are exactly the outcomes this pattern names, and a custom handler expresses anything else. Use the classic structure when the standard insertion modes cannot express your policy or you need per-item accounting.
code_sketch:
var q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<Msg>(10_000);          // a classic bounded buffer
if (!q.offer(msg)) dropped.increment();               // full: rejected, never blocked
var pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<Runnable>(1_000),
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());   // the full-policy as an object
pitfalls: add() throws IllegalStateException while offer() returns false: on a non-blocking path the wrong choice converts a shed decision into an uncaught exception.
An unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue in a ThreadPoolExecutor makes maximumPoolSize irrelevant: the queue absorbs the overload and the pool never grows.
DiscardOldestPolicy drops an already queued task, so a CompletableFuture someone is waiting on never completes - cancel or complete exceptionally when shedding.

variants.name: Flow.SubmissionPublisher with a drop handler
variants.implementation_notes: In reactive code the buffer belongs to the publisher: SubmissionPublisher is constructed with a per-subscriber maxBufferCapacity, submit blocks uninterruptibly until every subscriber has room, while the offer methods may drop - either immediately or after a bounded timeout - and invoke an onDrop handler so the loss can be logged, counted or retried. Choosing offer with an onDrop that returns false is the reject policy expressed as code the framework calls for you. Prefer this shape when the downstream already speaks Flow/reactive-streams and demand (request(n)) should drive the rate; the classic blocking queue remains the simpler tool for plain task pools.
variants.code_sketch:
var pub = new SubmissionPublisher<Msg>(executor, 10_000);   // per-subscriber buffer bound
pub.offer(msg, (sub, item) -> { dropped.increment(); return false; });  // false: give up
pub.subscribe(subscriber);                                   // request(n) drives the rate
pitfalls: The buffer is per subscriber: total memory is capacity x subscribers, not one capacity, so a fan-out silently multiplies the bound.
submit() blocks uninterruptibly while any subscriber lacks room - calling it from a latency-critical thread is a stall; use offer plus a drop handler there.
Close the publisher (close/closeExceptionally) on shutdown, or subscribers never see onComplete/onError and leak.
